claims.text: Atomic-size-mismatch strain energy can exceed configurational-entropy stabilization in near-equiatomic multielement nanoparticles at 773–1173 K.
Excess strain energy drives phase separation in these nanoparticles.
Excess strain energy drives surface segregation in these nanoparticles.
Only compositions with atomic-radius mismatch δ below approximately 5% remain single-phase and chemically homogeneous under the stated service conditions.
The proposed starting particles are 5–20 nm, near-equiatomic, single-phase solid solutions that are compositionally homogeneous before annealing.
The intervention compares equiatomic quinary nanoparticle compositions with δ≈3% and δ≈8%.
The two compositions can be made to differ only in δ.
Both nanoparticle compositions will be annealed at 1073 K for 10 h under inert Ar.
For the high-δ composition, elastic strain energy adds to positive mixing enthalpy.
For the high-δ composition, the combined energetic penalty overcomes T·ΔSmix and triggers phase separation and surface segregation.
For the low-δ composition, the energetic penalty remains below T·ΔSmix, preserving the solid solution.
After annealing, low-δ nanoparticles will remain single-phase and compositionally uniform.
After annealing, high-δ nanoparticles will develop additional XRD peaks indicating phase separation.
After annealing, high-δ nanoparticles will show surface elemental segregation by STEM-EDS and APT.
The proposed relationship applies to FCC near-equiatomic quinary nanoparticles of 5–20 nm in inert atmospheres at 773–1173 K.
The relationship may not apply to BCC alloys, δ outside 0–10%, particle sizes above 50 nm, or reactive-gas environments.
The critical δ threshold and its temperature dependence may vary with elemental combination and particle size.
Persistence of a single phase and chemical homogeneity in the δ≈8% nanoparticles after the specified anneal would falsify the hypothesis.
